analysis.one_liner: Requires federal regulators to cap how many commodity swap bets a single trader can hold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced October 1, 2008 with no cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that polices commodity markets, to set caps on how big a position any single trader can hold, counting together the trader's bets on registered exchanges, foreign exchanges, and large privately negotiated commodity derivatives known as "swaps." The point was to close a loophole: under the law at the time, a trader could exceed limits on an exchange by moving positions into the largely unregulated over-the-counter market. Legitimate hedging by businesses like airlines and farmers would have been exempt, and the agency could impose penalties of up to $1 million per violation, or the market value of the oversized position.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been consumers and businesses exposed to commodity prices, such as gasoline, heating fuel, and food, insofar as large speculative bets in the unregulated over-the-counter market were amplifying price swings. The bill's caps applied to the net sum of a trader's positions across exchanges and the OTC market, so speculators could no longer sidestep exchange limits by trading privately instead. Legitimate hedgers were explicitly exempt, so companies managing real physical risks would have kept unrestricted access.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the CFTC to set aggregate position limits on the net sum of a trader's positions across registered exchanges, foreign boards of trade, and large over-the-counter commodity derivatives, so a trader cannot dodge exchange limits by moving bets into the unregulated OTC market.
The stated purpose is to reduce the threat of market manipulation, excessive speculation, and congestion, protecting the price-discovery function of commodity contracts.
It gives the CFTC enforcement teeth: the power to order oversized positions reduced and to impose civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, or the market value of the excess position.
It exempts bona fide hedging transactions, so airlines, farmers, and other businesses hedging real physical risks keep full access to the markets.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on banks, swap dealers, hedge funds, and other large traders holding big speculative positions in the OTC commodity derivatives market. They would have faced caps on their net positions, possible orders to unwind oversized positions, and civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation or the market value of the excess position. Trading desks that profit from large speculative positions in oil and other commodities would have lost that freedom.

drawbacks.text: Position limits are hard to set correctly: if the CFTC sets them too tight, trading liquidity shrinks and hedging becomes more expensive for legitimate commercial users like airlines and food processors. The bill itself orders limits to be set only at the minimum level needed to keep hedging markets liquid, acknowledging this trade-off.

The bill leaves the CFTC broad discretion: the agency may decline to impose any limit on a class of OTC deals if it finds none of the listed factors apply, and it may let a violator keep an oversized position if forced unwinding would disrupt prices (charging a civil penalty instead). Whether the caps bite at all depends heavily on how the regulator exercises that discretion.

The bill's premise, that speculative OTC positions were distorting commodity prices, was contested at the time; the bill's own factors exclude bona fide hedging, meaning the caps target only the speculative share of the market, which may have been smaller than the 2008 price environment suggested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but conditional: closing the OTC loophole only helps if the CFTC actually writes and enforces the limits, and the bill gives it wide discretion to decline. The downside is that caps set too tight could shrink liquidity and raise hedging costs for legitimate commercial users, which is why the bill orders limits be set at the minimum level consistent with liquid hedging markets and exempts bona fide hedgers. On balance it is a modest, agency-driven fix rather than a hard cap, with bounded costs, but it never received committee or floor consideration, so its actual effect on anyone was zero.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The complete action history shows the bill was introduced on October 1, 2008, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, with no further action recorded.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and all bills not passed by then died, so the bill is not pending in any later Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Over-the-counter swap dealers and large speculators kept operating without aggregate position limits for the time being; consumers got no protection against speculation-driven commodity price swings. Congress later required similar limits in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, but this bill itself never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: OTC swap dealers and big speculators

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, so there is no roll-call to measure party support, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Over-the-counter swaps dealers and investment banks
industries.note: These dealers make money on large, largely unregulated OTC commodity derivative positions; the bill would put those positions under CFTC aggregate position limits and expose oversized bets to penalties up to $1 million per violation or the market value of the excess position. Their interest in keeping the OTC market unrestricted runs against consumers who bear the cost of speculation-driven price swings.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and large commodity speculators
industries.note: Traders taking very large speculative positions would face a cap on their net positions and could be forced to unwind them. The cap removes a tool for amplifying moves in oil and other commodity prices that show up in consumers' fuel and food costs.

Businesses hedging real physical risks are exempt as bona fide hedgers and would benefit from markets less prone to manipulation and congestion. Their interest runs alongside ordinary consumers', since steadier commodity prices feed into steadier retail prices.
